THOUGHT: The clinical picture—erythroderma with widespread sterile-appearing pustules since infancy, recurrent hospitalizations, systemic inflammation (fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, very elevated CRP/ESR)—is classic for generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP). The finding of a homozygous IL36RN mutation (c.115+6T>C) establishes deficiency of the IL-36 receptor antagonist (DITRA), a monogenic autoinflammatory cause of GPP that typically presents in childhood and produces flares with systemic features. Immunology showing markedly increased IL-17A–producing CD4+ T cells fits a psoriatic/Th17-driven mechanism. High-titer neutralizing anti-infliximab antibodies explain secondary biologic failure. Skin culture positive for Group B Streptococcus likely represents secondary colonization/infection of compromised skin rather than a primary cause. Taken together, the most likely diagnosis is DITRA-associated generalized pustular psoriasis; other differentials (sporadic GPP, drug-induced pustular eruptions such as AGEP or TNF-inhibitor–paradoxical pustular psoriasis, and primary bacterial pustular dermatoses) are less likely given the genetic and immunologic data and chronic course.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Deficiency of interleukin-36 receptor antagonist (DITRA) causing generalized pustular psoriasis (monogenic IL36RN-related GPP) — highest likelihood given homozygous IL36RN mutation, infant onset, systemic inflammation, and Th17 signature.
2. Generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch type) without identified mutation — clinically similar presentation; would be considered if genetic result were absent or variant significance uncertain.
3. TNF-inhibitor–associated paradoxical pustular psoriasis/drug-modified pustular psoriasis — possible contributor given anti-TNF therapy history, though neutralizing antibodies suggest loss of effect rather than classic paradoxical reaction.
4. Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) — drug-triggered pustular eruption with fever and neutrophilia; less likely because of chronicity since infancy and supportive genetic/immunologic findings.
5. Extensive bacterial pustular dermatitis with secondary erythroderma (e.g., widespread streptococcal/streptococcal-colonized pustular infection) — less likely as primary diagnosis given negative blood/urine cultures, chronic course from infancy, and genetic/immunologic evidence for autoinflammatory pustular psoriasis.
ground_truth: Deficiency of the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist (DITRA)
